whole-add.title: Adding whole numbers
whole-add.method: Model lining up ones, tens, and hundreds before adding. When a column reaches ten, show the exchange for one unit in the next place. Ask your student to explain what each regrouping mark represents.
whole-add.mistake: If your student forgets a regrouped ten, match the written work to tens and ones. Check that the new ten is included once in the next column.
whole-add.check: Have your student subtract one addend from the sum. Ask whether the result matches the other addend.

whole-sub.title: Subtracting whole numbers
whole-sub.method: Use place-value blocks to show the starting number. When there are not enough ones to subtract, exchange one ten for ten ones and record both changes. Model exchanges across a zero one place at a time.
whole-sub.mistake: If your student subtracts the smaller digit from the larger regardless of position, return to the starting collection. Show why the subtraction order must stay the same.
whole-sub.check: Ask your student to add the difference to the amount taken away. Together they should make the starting amount.

whole-mul.title: Multiplying whole numbers
whole-mul.method: Start with an area model or partial products. Name the value of each digit before multiplying, then connect each partial product to its place in the written algorithm.
whole-mul.mistake: If a tens partial product is misplaced, ask what the tens digit represents. Compare multiplying by two with multiplying by twenty.
whole-mul.check: Have your student estimate the product, then check by dividing by one factor. Discuss whether both checks support the answer.

whole-div.title: Dividing whole numbers
whole-div.method: Model long division using place-value units. At each step, discuss the amount being shared or grouped, then record the quotient digit, product, and difference. Show why a zero is sometimes needed in the quotient.
whole-div.mistake: If your student stops too early, check for a digit still to be brought down. If the remainder is at least as large as the divisor, show that another group can be made.
whole-div.check: Ask your student to multiply the quotient by the divisor and add the remainder. The result should equal the dividend.

decimal-add.title: Adding decimals
decimal-add.method: Use a place-value chart to line up decimal points. Show how trailing zeros can make equivalent places easier to see. Model regrouping from hundredths to tenths just as you would from ones to tens.
decimal-add.mistake: If your student lines up the right-hand digits instead of decimal points, label the place value of each digit before adding.
decimal-add.check: Have your student subtract an addend from the sum. Also compare the answer with an estimate using nearby whole numbers.

decimal-sub.title: Subtracting decimals
decimal-sub.method: Line up decimal points and model adding trailing zeros without changing the value. Show each exchange between neighboring places, recording the reduced digit as well as the added units.
decimal-sub.mistake: If your student changes the decimal point or forgets to reduce the place used for regrouping, compare the renamed number with the original amount.
decimal-sub.check: Ask your student to add the difference to the amount subtracted. The result should match the original starting amount.

decimal-mul.title: Multiplying decimals
decimal-mul.method: Use an area or scaling example to establish a reasonable product first. Then model whole-number multiplication and explain how the factors' decimal places determine the product's place value.
decimal-mul.mistake: If your student lines up decimal points as in addition, return to the size of the factors. Discuss why multiplying a positive amount by a number between zero and one makes it smaller.
decimal-mul.check: Have your student compare the product with the estimate. Division by a nonzero factor should give the other factor.

decimal-div.title: Dividing decimals
decimal-div.method: Show how multiplying both the dividend and divisor by the same power of ten leaves the quotient unchanged. Use a measurement example before connecting the idea to written division. Remind your student to round only when the question asks for it.
decimal-div.mistake: If your student shifts only one decimal point, compare the new quantities with the original problem. Both must be scaled by the same factor.
decimal-div.check: Ask your student to multiply the quotient by the original divisor. The product should equal the original dividend.

fraction-add.title: Adding fractions
fraction-add.method: Use matching fraction strips to establish equal-sized pieces. For unlike denominators, model renaming both fractions before adding the numerators. Discuss simplified fractions and equivalent mixed numbers when the sum is greater than one.
fraction-add.mistake: If your student adds denominators, point to the unchanged size of each piece. When renaming a fraction, show why the numerator and denominator must change by the same factor.
fraction-add.check: Have your student subtract one original fraction from the sum. Accept equivalent fractions that represent the other addend.

fraction-sub.title: Subtracting fractions
fraction-sub.method: Keep the same reference whole and show why the pieces must be the same size. Model a common denominator, then subtract the numerators. For mixed numbers, demonstrate conversion to improper fractions when helpful.
fraction-sub.mistake: If your student reverses the subtraction or changes only a numerator, return to the total and the part being removed in the model.
fraction-sub.check: Ask your student to add the difference to the fraction subtracted. Compare the result with the starting amount using equivalent fractions.

fraction-mul.title: Multiplying fractions
fraction-mul.method: Use an area model to show a fraction of another fraction. Connect the overlap to multiplying numerators and denominators. Show how to convert mixed numbers before calculating and simplify using common factors.
fraction-mul.mistake: If your student cancels matching digits, distinguish digits from factors. If a mixed number is multiplied in separate parts incorrectly, model its equivalent improper fraction first.
fraction-mul.check: Have your student estimate the product and explain its size. Division by a nonzero original factor should give the other factor.

fraction-div.title: Dividing fractions
fraction-div.method: Start with a sharing or measurement model so the quotient has meaning. Then connect the model to multiplying by the divisor's reciprocal. Convert mixed numbers before applying the procedure.
fraction-div.mistake: If your student flips the first fraction or both fractions, label the dividend and divisor. Use a simple example to check which reciprocal produces the correct quotient.
fraction-div.check: Ask your student to multiply the quotient by the original divisor. The product should equal the dividend.

round.title: Rounding decimals
round.method: Place the decimal between the two possible rounded values on a number line. Identify the midpoint, then connect the nearer endpoint to the digit rule. For these positive-number examples, explain that an exact midpoint rounds up.
round.mistake: If your student rounds in several stages, return to the original number and the requested place. Rounding an intermediate result can change the final answer.
round.check: Have your student name the two neighboring possible answers and explain which is closer to the original number.

detail-natural-add-2-2-regroup.intro: Use this worksheet to teach 2-digit addition with regrouping. Work through one example with your student before assigning independent practice. The first number has 2 digits, and the second has 2 digits.
detail-natural-add-2-2-regroup.condition: Every problem requires regrouping. Model how to record both parts of each exchange before assigning the worksheet.

detail-natural-add-2-2-no-regroup.intro: Use this worksheet to teach 2-digit addition without regrouping. Work through one example with your student before assigning independent practice. The first number has 2 digits, and the second has 2 digits.
detail-natural-add-2-2-no-regroup.condition: These problems do not require regrouping. Use them to check place-value alignment and the order of subtraction.

detail-natural-div-2-1-remainder.intro: Use this worksheet to teach 2-digit division with remainders. Work through one example with your student before assigning independent practice. The first number has 2 digits, and the second has 1 digit.
detail-natural-div-2-1-remainder.condition: Every problem has a remainder. Ask for a whole-number quotient and remainder, and discuss what the remainder represents.

examples.step: Check: 5 × 8 + 3 = 43. The remainder is smaller than 8.
Check: 9 × 9 + 6 = 87. The remainder is smaller than 9.

detail-natural-div-2-1-exact.intro: Use this worksheet to teach 2-digit division without remainders. Work through one example with your student before assigning independent practice. The first number has 2 digits, and the second has 1 digit.
detail-natural-div-2-1-exact.condition: These problems divide evenly. Have your student check each quotient with multiplication.

examples.step: Check: 40 × 2 + 0 = 80. The remainder is smaller than 2.
Check: 18 × 3 + 0 = 54. The remainder is smaller than 3.
